concepts.title: Independence vs. knowing the literature
concepts.one_liner: Balance the creative freedom of independent thinking with a thorough understanding of existing research literature.
concepts.content: Sometimes it is useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track, as this mindset allows you to explore directions no one else is pursuing. When doing so, it is often best to remain humble and simply state that you are trying out a new direction. However, it is equally important to remember that many smart people have worked on related problems and documented their results. You should avoid being caught unfamiliar with the large body of literature closely related to your work.
concepts.motivation_md: Researchers must navigate the tension between following established paths and forging new ones. This concept helps researchers maintain original thought without wasting time reinventing the wheel or ignoring critical context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use independent thinking to explore novel directions others might overlook.
 - Stay familiar with the existing literature to avoid repeating known mistakes or missing context.
 - Maintain a balance between creative isolation and scholarly awareness.

key_passage.text: It's also sometimes useful to remember that many smart people have worked on this and related problems and written their thoughts and results down in papers.

motivation.text: Don't be caught flat-footed with a large body of closely related literature that you aren't familiar with.

concepts.title: Building your personal brand
concepts.one_liner: Build a professional reputation by consistently delivering high-quality work, ideas, presentations, and software.
concepts.content: In a professional context, you have a personal brand. There are many impressions you want to build regarding this brand: that you always do great work, possess good ideas, deliver excellent talks, and write high-quality software. You should promote your brand and build a strong reputation by consistently behaving in the way you wish to be perceived.
concepts.motivation_md: Success in academia and industry depends not just on technical skill, but on how others perceive your reliability and expertise. Building a brand ensures your contributions are recognized and valued.
concepts.recap_md:
- Your personal brand is the sum of others' impressions of your work and conduct.
 - Consistently deliver high-quality outputs to establish a reputation for excellence.
 - Actively manage how you are perceived by the community through your professional behavior.

key_passage.text: You have a brand: you. There are many impressions you want to build up about your brand: that person always does great work, they have good ideas, they give great talks, they write wonderful software. Promote your brand. Build up a great reputation for yourself by consistently behaving in the way you'd like to be thought of.

concepts.title: Cultivate and play to your strengths
concepts.one_liner: Identify and cultivate your specific strengths, such as creativity, implementation, or theory, to maximize your impact.
concepts.content: Cultivate your strengths and play to those strengths. Some possible strengths include being broad in your knowledge, being creative, being a great implementer, or being highly skilled at theoretical work.
concepts.motivation_md: Research is diverse; no one is perfect at everything. Identifying where you naturally excel allows you to contribute more effectively to teams and projects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identify whether your strengths lie in theory, implementation, creativity, or breadth.
 - Focus your efforts on tasks where your specific skills provide the most value.
 - Actively develop these strengths to distinguish yourself in your field.

key_passage.text: Cultivate your strengths and play to those strengths. Some possible strengths include being broad, being creative, being a great implementer, or being great at doing theory.

concepts.title: Progress and specific reporting of failures
concepts.one_liner: Define progress broadly to include understanding failures, simplifying tasks, and dedicated learning.
concepts.content: When reporting issues, avoid simply stating that something doesn't work. Instead, analyze why it failed, whether it should have worked, if there is a simpler case that does work, and if the issue is general to the category. Try to identify the specific failure point or create an example that does work; at minimum, make it fail more clearly to help understand the system. Progress should be viewed broadly. It includes showing why a method fails, simplifying a task to get it started, or spending time reading to gain the necessary understanding for future advancement.
concepts.motivation_md: Effective communication between students and advisors requires moving beyond binary 'success/failure' reporting. Understanding why something failed is often as valuable as a success.
concepts.recap_md:
- Report failures with specific analysis of why they occurred and how they might be simplified.
 - Recognize that proving why something doesn't work is a valid form of progress.
 - Include learning and background research in your definition of productive work.

key_passage.text: Progress can include things like "I've shown why this doesn't work," "I've simplified the task to get it to start working," or "I spent the whole time reading because I know I have to understand this before I can make any progress."

question.text: Why doesn't it work? Why should it work? Is there a simpler case we can make work? Do you think it's a general issue that affects all problems of this category? Can you think of what's not working? Can you contort things to make an example that does work? At the very least, can you make it fail worse, so we understand some aspects of the system?

motivation.text: I love to hear about progress when I meet with students, but note that I have a very general notion of progress.

concepts.title: Collaboration and authorship in science
concepts.one_liner: Prioritize impactful team-based science and ensure authorship reflects all meaningful contributions to the research.
concepts.content: Science is generally a team sport where the insight, foundation, and impact of the work matter more than the number of people involved. It is better to be one of many contributors to a great paper than the sole author of an unimportant one. These collaborations often lead to lifelong professional friendships. Regarding authorship, everyone who contributed to the paper should be included. Contributions can take the form of experimentation, providing a seminal idea, assisting with writing, or even exploring a research direction that ultimately did not work. If authorship is unclear, it is best to ask the individual and respect their preference.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern research is complex and collaborative. Clear guidelines on communication and authorship help maintain healthy professional relationships and ensure fair credit.
concepts.recap_md:
- Value being part of a high-impact team over individual authorship on minor works.
 - Include as authors everyone who contributed through ideas, experiments, writing, or failed explorations.
 - Maintain open communication with collaborators and advisors to foster long-term professional bonds.

key_passage.text: Science is generally a team sport. What matters in a collaboration is whether the work is insightful, foundational, or impactful. Everyone who contributed to the paper should have their name on it.

motivation.text: The relationships formed through collaborations can become friendships that last over your career. It is much better to be one of 10 contributors to a great paper than to be the sole author on an unimportant paper.

concepts.title: Slow down to speed up
concepts.one_liner: The advice "slow down to speed up" suggests that taking time to verify assumptions and change one variable at a time leads to faster research progress.
concepts.content: The advice "Slow down to speed up" highlights the difference between structured classroom problems and the ambiguity of research. In research, there is no guaranteed right answer or immediate feedback. To succeed, one must take things slowly, verify assumptions, and deeply understand the program, algorithm, or proof. When conducting experiments, change only one thing at a time to ensure the outcome is interpretable. It may feel slow, but this methodical approach results in more progress than unguided trial and error. (see figure: Research advice for a bumper sticker.)
concepts.motivation_md: Research lacks the structured feedback of coursework, making it easy to waste time on uninterpretable experiments without a methodical approach.
concepts.recap_md: - Verify all assumptions and deeply understand the underlying algorithms or proofs.\n- Change only one variable at a time during experiments to ensure results are meaningful.\n- Methodical progress is ultimately faster than uncoordinated trial and error.

key_passage.text: Take things slowly. Verify your assumptions. Understand the thing, whatever it is—the program, the algorithm, or the proof. As you do experiments, only change one thing at a time, so you know what the outcome of the experiment means.

motivation.text: It may feel like you're going slowly, but you'll be making much more progress than if you flail around, trying different things, but not understanding what's going on.

concepts.title: Don't just say 'it doesn't work'
concepts.one_liner: Instead of simply stating that a system "doesn't work," researchers should identify the specific step where failure occurs and rule out potential causes.
concepts.content: Researchers should avoid simply stating that a system "doesn't work." Because complex systems fail if any single step in the chain is incorrect, it is more productive to narrow down the problem. A better report identifies the specific step where the failure occurs, demonstrates that preceding steps work as expected by showing their inputs and outputs, and lists potential causes that have been ruled out.
concepts.motivation_md: Vague failure reports provide no path forward; identifying the specific point of failure is essential for debugging complex research systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid vague statements about failure and instead pinpoint the specific step where a process breaks.\n- Validate that earlier steps are functioning correctly by checking their intermediate outputs.\n- Explicitly state which potential causes of failure have already been ruled out.

key_passage.text: What I want to hear instead is something like, "I've narrowed down the problem to step B. Until step A, you can see that it works because you put in X and you get Y out, as we expect. You can see how it fails here at B. I've ruled out W and Z as the cause."

motivation.text: Of course, it doesn't work. If there's a single mistake in the chain, the whole thing won't work, and how could you possibly go through all those steps without making a mistake somewhere?

concepts.title: Hard work and sustainability in research
concepts.one_liner: Success in research depends on hard work and sustainability, which is best achieved by choosing problems you love.
concepts.content: In graduate school, hard workers often pull ahead of those who rely solely on intelligence. However, this hard work must be sustainable. It is important to maintain a work/life balance, protecting time for relationships, service, and relaxation to ensure the longevity of the research effort. The key to working hard enough to succeed is to pick a topic you love; enjoyment of the problem naturally leads to the time investment required for mastery.
concepts.motivation_md: Research is a marathon that requires both intense effort and a sustainable pace to avoid burnout while achieving high-level results.
concepts.recap_md: - Hard work is often the deciding factor for success in research environments where everyone is smart.\n- Maintain a sustainable pace by balancing work with personal life and relaxation.\n- Choosing a research topic you love makes the necessary hard work feel natural and enjoyable.

key_passage.text: By now, everyone around you is smart. In graduate school, it's the hard workers who pull ahead.

question.text: How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?

motivation.text: you should work at a pace you can sustain, and you should refresh yourself by making time for the things that matter more than work, such as relationships, service, and relaxation. Perhaps the point is to protect your time so you will have enough time to do the research well.

concepts.title: Steering: Motors and rudders in research
concepts.one_liner: Research requires both "motors" (hard work) and a "rudder" (steering) to ensure that effort is directed toward the right problems.
concepts.content: Working hard is necessary but insufficient for research success; one must also "steer." While hard work provides the "motor" or drive, steering acts as the "rudder," involving periodic steps back to ensure one is working on the right problems. Time management techniques can be helpful tools for this steering process, helping researchers focus their energy on solving the most impactful problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Effort is wasted if it is directed at the wrong goals; researchers must balance raw productivity with strategic reflection.
concepts.recap_md: - Hard work provides the drive, but steering ensures that effort is applied to the right tasks.\n- Periodically step back from daily work to evaluate the direction and impact of the research.\n- Use time management strategies to prioritize solving the most important problems.

key_passage.text: We're like boats. We need motors—that's the part about working hard. But we also need a rudder for steering—that means stepping back periodically to make sure we're working on the right thing.

motivation.text: On the topic of steering, I find time management books to be very helpful. They teach you how to spend your time solving the right problems.

concepts.title: The value of simple toy models
concepts.one_liner: Simple toy models help researchers build intuition about complex problems by capturing their main ideas in a manageable format.
concepts.content: Simple toy models—the simplest models that capture a main idea—are invaluable for building intuition in research. For example, the color constancy problem involves estimating surface reflectance colors from the product of the reflectance spectrum and an unknown illuminant spectrum. A toy model for this is estimating scalars $a$ and $b$ from their product $y = a \times b$. This simple problem offers surprising richness, allowing one to think through loss functions and Bayesian decision theory (see @fig-toy). (see figure: A toy model for the color constancy problem: $y = a \times b$. The plot shows the possible solutions for $a$ and $b$ when $y=1$.) Having intuitions from toy problems allows researchers to figure out what will work by thinking it through with the model.
concepts.motivation_md: Complex problems can be overwhelming; toy models strip away non-essential details to reveal the core logic and build necessary intuition.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the simplest possible model that captures the core essence of a research problem.\n- Toy models allow for rapid intuition building and theoretical exploration of concepts like loss functions.\n- Developing intuition on simple cases helps predict what will work in more complex scenarios.

key_passage.text: With a good one, you can build up intuition about what matters, which is a big advantage in research.

motivation.text: Having the intuitions from working with toy problems gives you a big advantage in the research because you can figure out what will work by thinking it through with your toy model.

concepts.title: The parable of the two students
concepts.one_liner: The parable of the two students illustrates that strong researchers look for solutions near a failed proposal rather than just reporting the failure.
concepts.content: A parable describes the difference between a weak and a strong graduate student. When an advisor asks both to try a particular approach to a research problem, the weak student follows the instructions exactly, and if the solution fails, they simply report that failure. The strong student, however, starts with the advisor's request but, upon seeing it doesn't work, looks within an epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work and reports that solution. (see figure: The parable of the two students.)
concepts.motivation_md: This parable encourages proactive problem-solving and independence in research, rather than passive adherence to instructions.
concepts.recap_md: - Weak students report failures exactly as they occur without further investigation.\n- Strong students proactively search for nearby solutions when an initial approach fails.\n- Success in research often involves iterating on and improving initial proposals.

key_passage.text: The weak student does exactly what the advisor has asked. But the advisor's solution fails, and the student reports that failure. The strong student starts doing what the advisor has asked, sees that it doesn't work, looks around within some epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work, and reports that solution.

motivation.text: There is a weak and a strong graduate student. They are both asked by their advisor to try a particular approach to solving a research problem.
